That last possibility has created particular concern in Saxony-Anhalt, where the state intelligence service has classified the AfD branch as a confirmed right-wing extremist organization.
A state government would also represent Saxony-Anhalt in the Bundesrat, the chamber through which Germany’s states participate in federal legislation.

Although state governments cannot halt German weapons deliveries to Ukraine or lift sanctions on Russia, an AfD breakthrough would give the party executive power, Bundesrat representation and a stronger platform ahead of the 2029 federal election.

(Photo by John MACDOUGALL / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip Make us preferred on Google Germany enters a decisive month of state elections with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) closer to executive power than at any point in its history.
The latest projection gives the AfD 41%, almost twice the 20.8% it received in the previous state election in 2021.
From eastern protest party to national force The September elections form part of a longer rise.
State elections do not determine foreign policy, and Ukraine was not among the principal concerns reported by AfD voters in 2024.
The AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt parliamentary group has opposed Ukraine’s accession to NATO and the EU, rejected weapons deliveries, and backed continued use of Nord Stream 2.
The state party’s 2026 program goes even further, proposing that Ukrainians in Germany no longer be recognized as war refugees.
Meanwhile, the AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt program calls for closer economic and cultural relations with Russia and expanded Russian-language teaching in schools.
Winning a state election would not give the AfD control over German foreign policy.
One state could not overturn Berlin’s policy alone, but it could use its votes, ministries, and political platform to obstruct legislation and promote closer relations with Moscow.
For Ukraine, the immediate danger is not that Saxony-Anhalt will suddenly take control of German foreign policy.

It’s the possibility of the AfD gaining its first record of executive government, normalizing its pro-Russia program, and forcing every other party to respond to its success before the next federal election in 2029.
The party is also leading in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, which votes on Sept.
The AfD is not leading there, but its support has risen to approximately 18%, compared with 9.1% in the city’s 2023 repeat election.
The AfD received 10.4% in Germany’s 2021 federal election.
“The AfD has much greater popularity in the eastern, so-called new federal states than in the old ones,” Berlin-based journalist Nikolai Klimeniouk told Kyiv Post.

“It is understandable that anti-liberal populist forces gain support under such conditions.” Advertisement The same trajectory was identified after the AfD’s strong results in Saxony and Thuringia in 2024.
Advertisement The German government concluded that people acting for Russian state agencies were responsible.
Berlin responded by closing Russia’s consulate general in Bonn and terminating the agreement governing the Russian House cultural center in Berlin.
Despite Berlin’s announcement, the center can remain open until its governing agreement expires in June 2027.
What an AfD state government could actually do.
Advertisement A state government would nevertheless control institutions with substantial power over everyday life.

An AfD government could reshape school curricula, redirect cultural funding, alter integration programs, appoint senior civil servants, and place its own ministers above the state police and domestic intelligence service.
An AfD interior minister could oversee the same state agency that monitors the party.
Winning the most votes would therefore not automatically make AfD candidate Ulrich Siegmund state premier.
Two years later, the AfD is substantially stronger, its position toward Kyiv is unchanged, and the party is closer than ever to acquiring real state power.

Whether or not AfD ends up governing, the result is a blow to Merz, whose center-right party has led Saxony-Anhalt for 24 years.
AfD is the biggest opposition party in Germany's national parliament and is strongest in the formerly communist and less prosperous east, where Saxony-Anhalt is located.

Its regional branch in Saxony-Anhalt is one of several classified as a proven right-wing extremist group by the domestic intelligence agency, which points to members' denigration of migrants from Muslim countries, among other things.

AfD's national co-leader, Alice Weidel, described the result as "sensational." She said the party's "hand is outstretched to all who want to make Saxony-Anhalt better and move Germany forward." It may hope to attract defectors from other parties.
Krisztian Bocsi / Bloomberg via Getty Images Once previously AfD won a state election but didn't end up governing.

Siegmund has listed among his top priorities "a deportation offensive" and dropping incentives for people to come to Germany and "exploit our social system." He wants to initiate a long process to withdraw Saxony-Anhalt from the regional public broadcaster, citing concerns about "disinformation." AfD in Saxony-Anhalt wants to allow home schooling, which so far isn't permitted in Germany.
The influence there of Saxony-Anhalt, one of the smaller states in a nation of 83.5 people, is limited — it controls four of the 69 votes.

Omer Messinger / Getty Images A first state government would be the biggest prize in the anti-migration party's 13-year history, at a time of widespread discontent with a national government that has yet to persuade voters that it can get the country's sluggish economy moving.
Unlike other countries in Europe, modern Germany hasn't yet had a far-right or right-wing populist party leading a national, state or major-city government.
Its leader in a neighboring state appealed two convictions for knowingly using a Nazi slogan.
Marcus Golejewski/picture alliance via Getty Images AfD won 43.8% of the vote, more than double its showing five years ago in the region of 2.1 million people west of Berlin.
The BSW party, which has said it wouldn't elect either Siegmund or incumbent Sven Schulze as governor but criticizes the "firewall" against AfD, took 5.3% and five seats.
Schulze congratulated AfD on becoming the state's strongest political force and said that "we as the CDU will also have to deal with this result," without specifying how.
It opposes taxpayers' money being "given away" to Ukraine and says it would push to lift sanctions against Russia, but that isn't a matter state governments can decide.
